meta.note: Twelve methods are listed. Only methods whose published fee was read in an official or bank-published document in this session carry a computed fee. Every other fee column is left blank and flagged.

status_legend.LAWFUL: Permitted on its face by the reviewed rule, subject to the bank's own due-diligence and documents.
status_legend.CONDITIONAL: Permitted only if specific facts or documents exist; eligibility is not established for any particular person.
status_legend.REJECTED: Prohibited by the reviewed rule. Listed so the risk is visible, not as advice.

methods.name: Onshore bank conversion of documented current-account income, then outward SWIFT wire (SHA)
methods.scope: Foreign or domestic individual with lawful current-account RMB income and the source documents
methods.cap: No USD 50,000 cap on the document route; the bank reviews the transaction evidence.
methods.fee_label: HSBC China Premier/Advance outward TT, sender pays own bank charges (SHA)
pros: Expressly contemplated by the FX rules: identity plus transaction/source evidence, including tax documents where required.
No statutory limit on when the old income is converted.
Can be entrusted to another person with authorisation and documents if the holder is abroad.
At the tariff read here the sender-side fee is capped (CNY 500 + CNY 120 cable), so it does not scale with the amount.
cons: The bank's due-diligence decision is discretionary; missing contemporaneous proof of the original income is the usual failure point.
Tax vouchers may have to be obtained first (a PRC tax filing, not a conversion fee).
FX spread and any correspondent/intermediary deductions are not published in the tariff and remain unverified.
Nothing here establishes that any particular balance qualifies.
steps: Obtain the original evidence of the RMB income: contract, payroll records, invoices, tax payment certificates.
If PRC individual income tax was not withheld, settle the PRC filing at the competent tax authority and keep the certificate.
Ask the bank in writing which category it will book the conversion under and what document list it requires.
Complete the tax recordal only if the bank/payee structure requires it for a service-trade payment.
Instruct the conversion and the outward wire on the same visit; request the applied CNY/USD rate and an itemised fee slip.
Keep the exchange memo, the wire confirmation and the rate evidence: they are needed for US basis and reporting.

methods.name: Same wire with 'Pay Exact' (OUR) so the receiving bank charges are absorbed
methods.scope: Same as M01, when the US receiving bank must not deduct a fee
methods.cap: No amount cap in the tariff; CNY 200 per instruction at the bank read here.
methods.fee_label: HSBC China Premier/Advance outward TT with Pay Exact (OUR) at CNY 200
pros: The published tariff states the beneficiary receives the full USD proceeds, with any shortfall collected later.
Removes uncertainty about receiving-bank deductions for the principal.
Same document route as M01, so no additional eligibility test.
cons: Adds a fixed CNY 200 per instruction.
Any shortfall in overseas bank charges is still collected from the remitter afterwards.
Does not remove the FX spread, which is the larger cost at high amounts.
steps: Complete the M01 document and conversion steps.
At instruction, tick the 'Pay Exact' / OUR option.
Confirm on the receipt that OUR was recorded and that the fee slip shows the CNY 200 item.
Retain the confirmation showing the exact USD amount the beneficiary received.

methods.name: Outward wire through a Private Banking individual account
methods.scope: Private Banking individual customer of the same bank
methods.cap: No amount cap in the tariff.
methods.fee_label: HSBC China Private Banking individual outward TT and cable (both published free)
pros: The tariff read here publishes the telegraphic-transfer issuance fee and the cable charge as free for individual Private Banking customers.
Same eligibility and document route as M01.
cons: Requires Private Banking status, which the holder may not have.
Free sender fees do not mean free conversion: the spread is not published.
Third-party and correspondent charges are expressly excluded from the tariff.
steps: Confirm the account is booked as a Private Banking individual account.
Obtain the same document set as M01.
Instruct the wire and obtain the fee slip showing zero commission and zero cable.
Record the applied rate, since the fee saving is trivial next to the spread.

methods.name: Outward wire as a Premier Elite customer (service-fee exemption)
methods.scope: Customer who meets the bank's published Premier Elite conditions
methods.fee_label: Premier Elite service-fee exemption published in the tariff remark
pros: The tariff remark states Premier Elite and Premier Elite Passport customers enjoy the service-fee exemption.
No change to the documentary basis of the transfer.
cons: Eligibility conditions are set by the bank and were not verified for any person.
Exemption covers the service fee only; the spread and third-party charges are unaffected.
steps: Confirm in writing that the account carries Premier Elite status for the instruction date.
Request the exemption be applied to the instruction and shown on the fee slip.
Otherwise follow M01.

methods.name: Document-based conversion at a different mainland bank (fee schedule not read here)
methods.scope: Any mainland bank account, where the bank accepts the document set
methods.fee_label: Published tariff for this bank was not read in this session
pros: The FX rules apply to banks generally, so the same document route should be available at other banks.
A second bank may apply a different spread or a more experienced documentary review.
cons: No fee, spread or acceptance practice is published in this study for any other bank; the cost cells are blank, not zero.
Branch-level practice and document lists differ.
steps: Ask the second bank for its written document list and its all-in quote for the exact amount.
Compare the quoted CNY/USD rate against the published board on the same day.
Proceed only when the itemised quote is in hand.

methods.name: Annual USD 50,000 facilitation quota, in yearly tranches
methods.scope: Domestic individual, or a foreign individual holding a Foreign Permanent Resident ID
methods.cap: USD 50,000 equivalent per person per year.
methods.fee_label: Bank fee for quota-based purchase not read in this session
pros: Simple identity-based route inside the quota, without a transaction-by-transaction source review.
Available to a domestic individual or a PR-ID holder.
cons: A foreign individual without a PR ID is outside this route.
Splitting a balance across people or years to defeat the quota is a separate unlawful act.
Takes 8 calendar years for USD 400,000 even if everything else is perfect.
steps: Establish which category the holder falls into, in writing, before relying on this route.
Convert up to the quota each calendar year and wire it out.
Keep every conversion memo so the tranches can be traced.
Do not use family members' quotas to accelerate the schedule.

methods.name: Overseas ATM cash withdrawals on a mainland debit card
methods.scope: Cardholder with a domestic card and an overseas ATM
methods.cap: RMB 100,000 equivalent per person per civil year; RMB 10,000 equivalent per card per day.
methods.fee_label: ATM operator and card-issuer charges not read in this session
pros: Uses an existing card; no documentary review at the counter.
Useful for spending needs rather than moving a balance.
cons: Hard annual ceiling, and exceeding it blocks overseas cash withdrawal for the current and following year.
Requires many withdrawals and many years for large sums.
Cash still has to be deposited in the US and is subject to the USD 10,000 border-reporting rule if carried.
Card and ATM fees are not published in the documents read here.
steps: Check the card's own overseas withdrawal limit and fee with the issuer.
Withdraw within RMB 10,000 equivalent per card per day.
Track the cumulative civil-year total against RMB 100,000.
Deposit the cash in a US account and keep the withdrawal slips.

methods.name: Reconversion of unspent RMB using the original exchange memo
methods.scope: Only money that itself came from an earlier FX conversion
methods.cap: Original memo valid 24 months; ID-only handling up to USD 500/day (USD 1,000 at port facilities).
methods.fee_label: Fee not read in this session
pros: A clear rule with a defined document: the original exchange memo.
Small same-day amounts need only ID.
cons: Does not apply to RMB earned in China, which is the usual case.
The 24-month validity has usually expired for a long-stuck balance.
Small daily limits make it irrelevant for USD 400,000.
steps: Locate the original exchange memo and check its date.
Present ID and the memo at the bank within 24 months of the exchange.
For larger amounts, expect the bank to apply the general document route instead.

methods.name: Capital-account transfer: emigration, inheritance or property proceeds
methods.scope: Emigrating individual's pre-emigration assets; foreign citizen inheriting a PRC estate; qualifying property proceeds
methods.cap: Governed by the separate provisional rules; not re-read in this session.
methods.fee_label: Fee not read in this session
pros: A recognised route with its own rulebook rather than the current-account document route.
Can be the only route for genuinely capital-account money.
cons: Heavy documentation and approval steps; the specific rulebook was not verified here.
Timeline and acceptance vary by locality.
Estate and property paperwork is usually the real bottleneck.
steps: Identify whether the balance is capital-account money at all (property sale, inheritance, pre-emigration assets).
Obtain the SAFE local-branch document list for that category in writing.
Assemble the title, tax-clearance and identity documents.
Obtain approval before instructing any conversion.

methods.name: Third-party remittance apps or agents (Wise, Western Union, 'agents')
methods.scope: Only if the provider is lawfully operating in China for that corridor and the source documents are accepted
methods.cap: Provider-specific and mostly undocumented in official sources.
methods.fee_label: Provider fee and availability not verified in this session
pros: May be cheaper for small amounts if genuinely available.
Convenient interface.
cons: No official PRC source read here confirms availability, limits or legality of any named provider for a mainland CNY balance.
Providers generally exclude third-party or business payments and require the money to be the sender's own salary.
Costs are blank in this study because nothing was verified.
steps: Check the provider's own China eligibility page and ask whether it operates for a mainland CNY balance.
Ask the bank whether the payment would be booked as a lawful current-account remittance.
Treat any quote as indicative until the receiving amount in USD is confirmed.

methods.name: REJECTED: cryptocurrency / USDT / stablecoin bridge
pros: Advertised as fast and outside the banking system.
cons: RMB-to-virtual-currency business is classified as illegal financial activity and must be strictly prohibited.
Banks and payment institutions may not provide accounts, transfers or settlement for it.
Counterparty, seizure and fraud risk sits entirely on the holder.
PRC FX penalties can reach 30% or more of the amount.
steps: Do not use this route.

methods.name: REJECTED: underground banking, '对敲' peer swaps, or splitting quotas across relatives
pros: Usually presented as avoiding documentation entirely.
cons: Private or disguised trading in foreign exchange is penalised at up to 30% of the amount, or more in serious cases.
Using other people's quotas to evade the annual limit is a separate evasion.
No legal recourse if the counterparty keeps the money.
Creates a US reporting problem on top of the PRC one.
steps: Do not use this route.
